speaker: DOJ & DHS (joint)
org: Department of Justice / Department of Homeland Security
venue: Interim Final Rule, 6 CFR & 28 CFR Part 124 (Docket FBI-2026-0001), effective 2026-07-01
quote: The Departments expect the initial Authorized Technologies List to include radio frequency (“RF”) detection with command-and-control signal interception, RF disruption ... and RF protocol manipulation
points: Two-tier SLTT certification: Detection & Warning, and Mitigation (hands-on at FBI NCUTC, Huntsville).
SLTT ops are limited to categories on an interagency Authorized Technologies List (and an Authorized Systems List as populated), distributed via FBI LEEP.
The initial list is expected to be RF-only: detection with C2 interception, jamming, and cyber takeover/command injection.

§124.17: in-flight physical interception ('catching or netting an aircraft in flight') counts as mitigation and requires Mitigation Certification; suspected explosive payloads go to HDS-accredited bomb squads.
FCC authorization required for RF-emitting systems; comments were due ~Sept 4, 2026.
um_relevance: CRITICAL NUANCE: physical capture is recognized but is not expected on the initial SLTT technology list. Before UM can sell to state and local police, a physical-interception category likely needs to be added through the interagency process. That is a policy engagement task, not a sales task. Federal (DHS/DOJ under 6 U.S.C. 124n) and DoD (10 U.S.C. 130i) users are not bound by this list.

speaker: Rep. Rick Larsen (D-WA)
role: Ranking Member, House Transportation & Infrastructure Committee
quote: significantly expanding use of high-risk counter-UAS technologies with lax safety guardrails
points: Objected to the administration inserting its own C-UAS language into the FY26 NDAA instead of the bipartisan tri-committee H.R. 5061.
Warned it minimizes the FAA's safety role.
um_relevance: Aviation-safety stakeholders (T&I, FAA) remain a brake on domestic mitigation. A low-collateral capture effector is the easiest mitigation story to sell to them.

speaker: U.S. Navy (NAVSEA/PEO)
venue: Request for white papers: Naval Affordable Interceptor Prototype
points: Containerized launcher holding at least 60 interceptors; installable without permanent ship modification.
Operational capability within 12 months of award; production path of at least 500 interceptors/yr.
Targets drones and cruise missiles; driven by Red Sea magazine depletion.
um_relevance: Out of scope for UM's Block 1 (missile-class). It confirms 'containerized and portable' as a cross-service buying theme — a point in favor of UM's canister launch.

speaker: Department of War Comptroller
quote: $20.6 billion for Counter-Unmanned Systems (C-UXS), including $14.4 billion associated with the Drone Dominance mandatory funding request
points: $20.6B, up $16.6B or 424% over FY26 enacted ($3.9B); $14.4B of it is the mandatory 'Drone Dominance' request (budget overview book, generated 20 Apr 2026).
JIATF-401's own RDT&E line (PE 0205401JCA, Counter-Small UAS): $6.5M in FY26 (mandatory only) rising to $580.348M in FY27, then about $581M in FY28–29 and about $101M in FY30.
Army lines: C-UAS Development (0605347A) $140.4M → $359.2M; C-sUAS Advanced Technology (0603135A) $7.8M → $156.5M; C-sUAS Applied Research (0602135A) $12.6M → $26.5M. Navy C-UAS (0604636N) $20.8M.
JIATF-401 sits in the Joint Staff as a Chairman's Controlled Activity; the Secretary of the Army, as Executive Agent, holds its acquisition authority.
Army small C-UAS procurement request $994M (FY26 enacted $596M).
um_relevance: The JIATF-401 line is RDT&E funding for rapid prototyping, integration and testing of C-sUAS — the money most suited to an early-stage interceptor. It holds at about $580M a year through FY29 in the request. Army C-UAS advanced technology jumps 20x, another prototype-stage source.

speaker: House Appropriations Committee
quote: $1.4 billion for the Joint Interagency Task Force 401 (JIATF 401)
points: $1.4B for JIATF-401, including a new $580M counter-UAS prototyping line.
$1B for the Defense Autonomous Warfare Group (DAWG); $1.1B for DIU; $600M APFIT.
New flexibility lets DAWG/JIATF-401 R&D funds pay for procurement, production and O&M.
$50M for US-Israel directed energy / C-UAS.
um_relevance: The $580M prototyping line is the most UM-relevant money in the federal budget: R&D funds that can buy prototypes and early production without a new program of record.

speaker: HASC & SASC
quote: Establishes Robotic and Autonomous Systems Combatant Command (RASCOM) (Senate §917, paraphrase)
points: SASC $1.14T / HASC $1.15T toplines.
Senate §1044 drone posture review; §847 expands restricted UAS components list; §1216 raises US-Israel C-UAS cooperation to $100M/yr; House §1223 extends US-Israel C-UAS cooperation through Dec 2029.
House §834 Autonomy Integration Account.
um_relevance: Supply-chain restrictions (§847) favor US-built components; keep UM's BOM free of covered-country parts from day one.

speaker: President Donald Trump
venue: Signing of FY26 NDAA (P.L. 119-60), Title LXXXVI SAFER SKIES Act
points: Extends C-UAS authority to trained, certified SLTT law enforcement and corrections.
§8603-8604: UAS/C-UAS eligible under federal grant programs.
§8606: DHS standards for safe and lawful drone-interception training.
Mitigation reports due to DOJ/DHS within 48 hours.
um_relevance: Creates the SLTT market (18,000+ agencies), but entry depends on the authorized-technology list (see IFR).
